<reason>Both sides were excellent, but B built the stronger path. A's spine was a dilemma: the notice is either useless or indefensible. B threaded it—showing a bare existence-notice does real work (ends false certainty, forecast-vs-verdict dignity, triggers complaints/audits, enables a differentiating market) without individualized disclosure. B also handled pressure better: A's Q2 trap ("name the app or concede") was turned into the market-creation case, later sealed by the "different label" point. B's closing broke A's "informative = gameable" dilemma via the credit-score distinction and turned A's checkpoint analogy against A (users are the screened, not threats)—points A's closing left unanswered despite speaking last. A landed real hits (the consolation "shrink," Prop 65, identical labels, licensed-fact gaming), but after endorsing regulator-facing disclosure, A's position reduced to "the ranked person is the one party who mustn't be told," which B exploited cleanly.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's A2—"I can't name the app, and that is the strongest case for the motion"—converted A's sharpest pressure question into the core of PRO's market argument, and B's closing checkpoint-analogy takedown plus meaning-vs-exploitability (credit score) dissolved A's central dilemma unrepaired.</best_rebuttal>
